problems.description: Rendered markdown HTML (marked.parse output) is inserted into pageTemplate/indexTemplate raw with no sanitization; marked does not sanitize by default, so raw HTML in source markdown is an XSS vector.

parseSimpleYaml is a hand-rolled YAML parser that only handles flat key:value frontmatter; nested keys, inline comments, and values containing ':' will be silently misparsed. Inconsistent with the codebase already depending on gray-matter and marked for the same concerns.

The entire generator (parsing, templating, file IO, sorting) is monolithic in index.ts with no module separation; SonarQube records +6 smells and +50 cognitive complexity, concentrated in giant template-literal functions.
Greenfield commit ships no tests despite the seed's 'good seams' precedent; parsing, escaping, and path mapping logic are exactly the kind of edge-case code that needs coverage.
The 'intentionally no YAML engine' rationale conflicts with adopting gray-matter (which already parses YAML frontmatter) — the custom parser adds risk without removing a dependency.

strengths: Clean typed interfaces (Frontmatter, Page, BuildOptions, ParsedMarkdown) and small pure functions make the core logic readable and testable in isolation.
Modern async node:fs usage with a recursive, deterministically sorted directory walk and proper path normalization to URL-style output paths.
Sensible fallback behavior for title/tags/date frontmatter rather than crashing on missing fields.
commit_reviews.summary: A workable greenfield static site generator, but the hand-rolled YAML parser, unsanitized markdown output, and monolithic index.ts introduce real technical debt that later sessions will pay for.

problems.description: Reimplements a Handlebars subset with an ordering-sensitive, regex-based engine (each/if/partial/triple-stash interpolation) that recursively re-parses sources per page; mechanical delta supports the concern (smells +2, cognitive complexity +39).

templateContext spreads frontmatter then page, so Page fields (date, tags, html) can silently shadow frontmatter values, and the whole raw `page` object is exposed to templates; collisions are deterministic but easy to trip on.

Measured convention score 0.52 with 26 violations, but nearly all listed violations are in files/lines untouched by this diff (e.g., dev-server.ts var/snake_case), while the diff's own additions are camelCase/PascalCase-conformant — qualitative judgment disagrees with a repo-level baseline here.
New tests cover the happy path (template + layout + partials) but not the backward-compat fallbacks (missing templatesDir, unknown template name falling back to pageTemplate, missing partial).
Templates are loaded once per build (good), but renderTemplate does multiple full-string regex passes and recursively re-renders partials per page; acceptable at this scale, not scalable.

strengths: Fully backward compatible: absent templatesDir/template falls back to the existing pageTemplate/indexTemplate output, so current behavior is preserved.
Respects existing patterns: extends BuildOptions, the buildSite render loop, and parseArgs' CLI flag handling consistently (--templates).
Escaped {{ }} interpolation with escapeHtml while {{{ }}} stays raw — sensible XSS posture for a template engine.
Tests added in the existing suite covering templates, layouts, and partials end-to-end.
commit_reviews.summary: A backward-compatible, pattern-respecting templating feature with tests that slots cleanly into the existing build flow, though its regex-based mini engine adds notable complexity (+39 cognitive, 2 smells) against an already-weak convention baseline.

problems.description: Duplicates the dev-server implementation that already exists in src/plugins/dev-server.ts from a prior session — this 'integration' commit builds a second, divergent dev server inline in index.ts instead of wiring the existing one, leaving two implementations to drift.

injectLiveReload's idempotency guard checks for `new WebSocket('ws://' + location.host)` (spaces around +) but injects `'ws://'+location.host` (no spaces) — the guard never matches, so it is dead code and repeated calls double-inject the script.
decodeURIComponent(request.url) in serveFile runs before the try/catch — a malformed URL (e.g. '/%zz') throws URIError and becomes an unhandled rejection that can crash the server.

liveReloadScript const violates the project's UPPER_CASE constant convention; post-commit convention score is 0.52. Note the bulk of the 26 measured violations are attributed to dev-server.ts, which is NOT part of this diff (pre-existing), so the commit's own convention delta is smaller than the measurement implies.

Watcher rebuilds have no debounce/delay — chokidar emits many events per save and the rebuilding/queued flag only collapses one extra rebuild, so rapid multi-file saves trigger cascading full rebuilds.
Only injectLiveReload got a unit test; the actual server behavior (serveFile, path-traversal 403s, WS upgrade, rebuild-on-change, close()) appears uncovered.
parseArgs return type widened from BuildOptions to ServeOptions, changing the exported public signature (benign within the project but observable to consumers).

strengths: Path-traversal protection: serveFile serves only paths resolved under the output root (403 otherwise).
Reuses buildSite for both initial build and rebuilds — serving is layered on the existing pipeline, no build logic duplicated.
Clean DevServer lifecycle: close() tears down watcher, WS clients, HTTP server, and WS server in order.
Rebuild throttling via rebuilding/queued flags prevents overlapping concurrent rebuilds.
Follows existing CLI conventions: extends parseArgs, dispatch on subcommand in main(), caret-versioned deps matching package.json style.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured, security-conscious dev-server + live-reload feature that fits the SSG's build pipeline, but it duplicates an existing dev-server plugin from a prior session and carries minor defects (a never-matching idempotency guard, an unguarded decodeURIComponent), with the 0.52 convention score largely reflecting pre-existing dev-server.ts violations rather than this diff.

problems.description: 26 convention violations (score 0.52): snake_case functions in TypeScript, non-PascalCase classes/interfaces, non-UPPER_CASE constants, and `var` usage in dev-server.ts — all regressions vs. the original index.ts which used camelCase functions and PascalCase types.
Cognitive complexity increased +5 and SonarQube smells +7 despite this being a refactor — the split added code (+258 lines, +184 imports) rather than simplifying the logic.
+184 imports across 5 new files suggests over-fragmentation; a 369-line module split into 5 files may spread cohesive logic too thinly without a clear module boundary.

strengths: Monolithic 369-line index.ts decomposed into 5 focused files, improving separation of concerns.
Preserved the project's deliberate no-YAML-engine decision (gray-matter comment carried forward), respecting a documented architectural constraint.
No new bugs (bugs +0) and zero duplication introduced.
commit_reviews.summary: The refactor modularizes the monolith (a genuine architectural win) but regresses on TypeScript conventions and increases cognitive complexity, so on net it lands worse than the original.

problems.description: Cache-skip path breaks buildSite's contract: for unchanged pages the onFile hook never runs, so context.pages[i].html is left unpopulated/stale while the rendered HTML lives only in the manifest. Callers that consume the returned Page[] (dev server, watch mode) would serve empty or stale markup after an incremental build.

Incremental-cache correctness silently depends on undocumented plugin metadata keys (context.metadata.sourceHashes, context.metadata.markdownContent). Nothing in the typed BuildContext/plugin contract guarantees they are populated, so caching can silently degrade or skip rebuilds based on an implicit, cross-cutting contract between the core loop and the markdown plugin.

Bypassing the onFile hook for cached pages changes plugin semantics globally: any plugin that relies on onFile running per page (asset handling, live-reload registration, analytics) silently stops firing under incremental mode. Caching is embedded in the core loop rather than composed through the hook lifecycle it bypasses.

+34 cognitive complexity in one commit; the dense single-line style (nested ternaries, inline awaits in the unchanged/skip and manifest-write statements) makes the build loop hard to read, matching the +4 SonarQube smells.
+0 files and no tests added for a 111-line caching feature; cache hit/miss, invalidation on template/source change, and the removed-page cleanup path are all uncovered.
console.log in a library entrypoint; build-stats output should be optional/injectable rather than hardcoded side-channel logging.

Cache key covers only template + source hashes; changes to configFile or plugin behavior do not invalidate the cache, so stale output can survive config/plugin changes (beyond the rm'd-outputDir force path).

strengths: Graceful degradation: readManifest and hashFiles tolerate missing/malformed cache (ENOENT and JSON parse are handled) rather than crashing the build.
Removed-source cleanup is handled: pages present in the previous manifest but absent from the current source set get their outputs rm'd.
The invalidation model (templateHash + sourceHash + output-existence check) is a sensible first-pass cache key, and the incremental && !clean semantics are coherent.
Feature matches the 'cross_cutting' session theme and integrates via the existing hooks/metadata seam rather than a new subsystem.
commit_reviews.summary: A legitimately themed incremental-cache feature that fits the hook lifecycle stylistically, but its cache-skip path leaves returned Page.html unpopulated and leans on undocumented plugin metadata contracts, while the measured convention score of 0.52 largely reflects pre-existing dense-style/naming hits that the added code perpetuates rather than newly introduces.

compounding_issues: Session 1 (greenfield) discarded the Express Todo-API seed almost entirely and pivoted to a markdown SSG, so the seed's 'good seams' provided no real runway and session 1 rebuilt the codebase from zero

The zero-dependency decision (hand-rolled parseSimpleYaml frontmatter parser + regex-based Handlebars-style template engine) created a persistent constraint that every later session had to work around and never got replaced by a mature engine
Session 3 embedded the dev server (HTTP + WebSocket + chokidar) directly into index.ts, inflating it to ~400 lines and forcing session 4's large 369-line-delete extraction refactor

The regex template engine's output is HTML-escaped by default and relies on recursion for nesting, limiting expressiveness for subsequent feature work (e.g., no helper functions, no layout inheritance beyond hand-rolled partials/layouts)
key_decisions: Session 1 pivot: rebuild as a markdown-to-HTML static site generator (gray-matter + marked) with a deliberately zero-dependency custom YAML frontmatter parser
Session 2: hand-rolled regex-based template engine supporting {{#each}}/{{#if}}/partials/layouts with contextual escaping rather than adopting an existing template library
Session 3: integrated dev experience — chokidar file watching, WebSocket live-reload injection, and an HTTP server with explicit path-traversal protection

Session 4: extraction into a plugin architecture with lifecycle hooks (onStart/beforeBuild/onFile/afterBuild/onEnd), PluginFactory + config-file loading, and dependency-injected build callback (DevServerPlugin receives build()) to avoid circular imports

Session 5: incremental builds via SHA-256 content hashing, a .ssg-cache.json manifest, template-hash invalidation, stale-page cleanup, and build stats — layered cleanly onto the plugin/metadata system
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved across the five sessions with a clear arc of accumulation → correction → refinement. Sessions 1–3 rapidly added features (SSG core, templating, live dev server) while index.ts bloated toward ~400 single-file lines, so structural quality degraded as capability grew. Session 4 was a decisive corrective refactor that shrank index.ts to ~46 lines and generalized the pipeline behind a plugin interface, which directly paid off in session 5: the incremental-build caching feature landed as a clean, well-scoped cross-cutting addition rather than more single-file sprawl. Test discipline held throughout — every session added tests (17 total, covering parsing, templating, plugin hook ordering, live-reload injection, CLI parsing, and incremental rebuild behavior) — and the refactor preserved all prior behavior while making the final feature easy to add.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent build-up in which an initially messy single-file SSG was corrected by a mid-story plugin refactor that enabled a clean cross-cutting incremental-build finale — a strong example of improving (not degrading) quality across sessions.
